clue.text: There's such method in the dialogue

definitions.text: There's such method in the dialogue

parts.words: There's such method in the dialogue
parts.note: the clue describes an adjective that names both a questioning method of teaching and the philosophical dialogues of Plato's teacher

explanation.surface: A remark that there is method behind what is being said in a conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Method in the dialogue' sounds like the idiom 'method in his madness', but both nouns pair with the adjective: the questioning method and the dialogues Plato wrote about his teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato's teacher gave his name to both the question-and-answer teaching method and the dialogues in which he appears.

clue.text: Yard of France

parts.note: Scotland Yard is London's police headquarters, and France has its own detective branch long called by an English form of its name

explanation.surface: A measure of length belonging to France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yard' looks like a unit of length; it is Scotland Yard, the London police. The French Sûreté was long written in English as the Surety.
explanation.definitionFit: The French criminal-investigation police, the Sûreté, filled the role in France that Scotland Yard plays in London.

clue.text: Skinning the hare — or looking over the joint

definitions.meaning: to case an animal is an old hunting word for stripping off its skin
to case the joint is slang for reconnoitring a place before robbing it

explanation.surface: A cook skinning a hare, or else sizing up the roast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The joint' looks like a cut of meat beside the hare, but it is a building a burglar inspects.
explanation.definitionFit: Stripping an animal's skin and checking out premises before a burglary are both called by this word.

clue.text: Gastronomically divine

parts.note: food fit for the gods, like the fabled food of Olympus

explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosia was the food of the Greek gods, so a dish tasting heavenly is described with its adjective.

clue.text: A fine time to be late !

definitions.text: A fine time to be late !

parts.words: A fine time to be late
parts.note: a spell of fine weather arriving late in the year, in autumn

explanation.surface: A sarcastic remark to someone who has turned up late at a bad moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A fine time to be late!' sounds like a rebuke; read literally it is a spell of fine weather that comes late, in autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: A warm spell of sunny weather in autumn, after summer has properly ended, has this name.

clue.text: With which Howard leaves the board ?

definitions.text: With which Howard leaves the board ?

parts.words: With which Howard leaves the board
parts.note: Howard is the Welsh novelist whose surname is the word wanted, and a diver leaves the board with a jump of that name

explanation.surface: A question about how a man called Howard resigns from a company board.
explanation.walkthrough: The board sounds like a boardroom, but it is a diving board. Howard Spring was a Welsh novelist (Fame is the Spur), so the word completes his name and also names the leap off the board.
explanation.definitionFit: A jump or leap is what takes a diver off the board, and the same word is the surname of the novelist Howard.

clue.text: A fidgety character when without a bottle

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the name goes round the single letter

parts.note: Fidgety Phil (Philip) is the boy who cannot sit still at table in the cautionary verses of Struwwelpeter

explanation.surface: Someone who gets restless when deprived of the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a drinker fidgeting without alcohol. 'without' means outside here: Fidgety Phil, from the German children's book Struwwelpeter, goes round A.
explanation.definitionFit: A phial is a small glass bottle, especially for medicine.

clue.text: Print with die, producing thus bold type

definitions.note: describes a fearless kind of person, so an adjective stands for the noun phrase

indicators.note: the two words are worked over to produce, in this way, a new arrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: Printing with a die to produce bold type.
explanation.walkthrough: The printing words make 'bold type' look like heavy typeface; it is a fearless sort of person.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fearless and daring is described as intrepid.

clue.text: Get rates adjusted to the maximum

definitions.note: the noun phrase stands for the superlative adjective, the most of anything

indicators.note: adjusted means the letters of the two words are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: Push the charges up as far as they will go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adjusted' rearranges GET RATES, and the surface is of tax rates raised to the top.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest or highest amount possible is the superlative of 'great'.

clue.text: Tempus fugit one gathers …

parts.note: time flies, so as Herrick's poem urges, one gathers these flowers while one may

explanation.surface: A Latin tag about time flying, left trailing off as someone gathers something.
explanation.walkthrough: Herrick's poem 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' begins 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may, / Old Time is still a-flying': the clue sets the Latin for 'time flies' beside what the poem tells you to gather.
explanation.definitionFit: Herrick's line tells young people to gather young roses while they can, because time is flying.

clue.text: Not a jot — but seldom far from it

definitions.text: Not a jot — but seldom far from it

parts.words: Not a jot — but seldom far from it
parts.note: the phrase 'every jot and ...' means the word wanted is not jot itself but its usual partner

explanation.surface: Insisting something is not the slightest bit, yet almost so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a jot' reads as 'not at all', but it says the word is not 'jot' while it seldom strays far from jot, as in the phrase 'every jot and tittle' (from Matthew 5:18).
explanation.definitionFit: A tittle is a tiny written mark, the small dot or stroke paired with jot in the biblical phrase about every last detail.

clue.text: News item includes article on substantive building material

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
substantive is the grammarian's word for a noun
cement is a building material

explanation.surface: A news report that includes a piece on solid construction materials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'substantive' looks like an adjective meaning solid, but it is the grammar term for a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A public statement giving news is a declaration or notice.

clue.text: King Cole turns to leave the dance

indicators.note: turns tells us the name taken from the singer is read from its last letter back to its first

parts.note: the singer Nat King Cole, so King Cole suggests his first name Nat
to go means to leave

explanation.surface: Old King Cole, the merry monarch of the nursery rhyme, turning to leave the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery-rhyme Old King Cole is the false trail; the King Cole meant is the singer Nat King Cole. 'turns' reverses NAT to give TAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a ballroom dance from Argentina.

clue.text: What happened to the marriage that never was?

definitions.text: What happened to the marriage that never was?

parts.words: What happened to the marriage that never was
parts.note: a marriage that legally never existed has been declared void by a court

explanation.surface: A wistful question about the fate of a wedding that was called off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a wedding that never took place; the legal reading is a marriage declared void, so that in law it never existed.
explanation.definitionFit: Declaring a marriage void makes it as if it had never legally existed.

clue.text: Their objective the stars bringing light to darkest Africa ?

definitions.note: describes the people who do the bringing, so a phrase defines a plural noun

parts.note: an objective is a mission
Aries, the Ram, is a constellation and sign of the zodiac, one group of stars

explanation.surface: Explorers who aim for the stars, bringing enlightenment to the continent once called darkest Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Darkest Africa' is the old colonial phrase; the light brought is the Christian gospel. 'the stars' gives a constellation, the Ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Evangelists sent abroad by churches were said to bring the light of the gospel to Africa.

clue.text: Hill of Mars

parts.note: Mars is the Roman name for the Greek war god Ares, whose hill in Athens gave its name to the council that met there

explanation.definitionFit: The rocky hill in Athens named after Ares, the Greek Mars, was also the seat of an ancient court.

clue.text: Unintentional result of that psychological thing in stress

indicators.note: in means the psychological term sits inside the word for stress

parts.note: an accent is stress laid on a syllable
the id is Freud's term for the instinctive part of the psyche

explanation.surface: An unplanned outcome of a psychological condition brought on by stress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stress' reads as anxiety, matching the psychology, but it is the stress on a syllable, an accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishap that happens unintentionally, without anyone planning it, is called this.

clue.text: He's sent to find a girl in a year perhaps

indicators.note: in places the girl inside the rearranged letters of the year
perhaps suggests the letters of year may take another arrangement

parts.note: miss is a word for a girl or young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A man dispatched to track down a girl within the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a girl in a year' reads as a search lasting twelve months; 'perhaps' signals that the letters of 'year' are to be rearranged, and 'in' sets the girl among them.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoy or agent is someone dispatched on another's behalf.

clue.text: Praised, but made remarks about the twisted lip

indicators.note: about tells us the remarks wrap round the twisted letters, sitting on either side of them

parts.note: to make remarks is to comment, past tense commented

indicators.note: twisted says the three letters of lip are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone was praised, yet made comments about a curled lip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the twisted lip' suggests a sneer being remarked on; 'twisted' rearranges the lip's letters and 'about' wraps the remarks round them, splitting that word in two.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay someone a flattering remark is to praise them.

clue.text: Rossini's factotum

parts.note: the barber in Rossini's opera The Barber of Seville, who sings the aria 'Largo al factotum'

explanation.definitionFit: The barber-hero of The Barber of Seville introduces himself as the town's factotum, the man who does everything.

clue.text: Burning emblem of a playful Grocer Errant

definitions.text: Burning emblem of a playful Grocer Errant

parts.words: Burning emblem of a playful Grocer Errant
parts.note: Beaumont's play The Knight of the Burning ... has a grocer's apprentice playing a knight errant with a burning ... as his device

explanation.surface: A heraldic badge, on fire, for a comic grocer who goes questing like a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: In Francis Beaumont's comedy The Knight of the Burning Pestle (1607), a grocer's apprentice, Rafe, plays a knight errant whose device is a burning pestle, the grocer's tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A grocer's pounding tool, used with a mortar, appears ablaze as the knightly emblem in Beaumont's play.

clue.text: Some bargains in cereals are not genuine

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some of the bargain offers on breakfast cereals are fake.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts at the end of 'bargains', takes all of 'in', and ends inside 'cereals'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something insincere is not heartfelt, a pretence rather than real feeling.

clue.text: Many long legs are seen in it

definitions.text: Many long legs are seen in it

indicators.note: seen in says the letters wanted are on view inside the words before them

explanation.surface: Plenty of long legs are on display in some garment or material.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across 'maNY LONg'; read whole, the clue is the stocking material in which many long legs are seen.
explanation.definitionFit: Synthetic stockings are so often made of this fibre that they are named after it.

clue.text: Number the best years of your life

definitions.meaning: a whole number divisible only by itself and one

definitions.text: the best years of your life
definitions.meaning: the peak period of life, when one is at one's best

explanation.surface: Counting off the finest years of a lifetime.
explanation.definitionFit: A number with no divisors but one and itself has this name, and so does the period when a person is at their peak.

clue.text: Supply with power

parts.note: to give someone the means or capacity to do something

explanation.definitionFit: To give someone the means or authority to act is to empower them.

clue.text: "This fell, death, Is strict in his arrest " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "This fell, death, Is strict in his arrest " (Hamlet)

parts.words: "This fell, death, Is strict in his arrest " (Hamlet)
parts.note: the missing word in Hamlet's dying speech is the officer who makes an arrest

explanation.surface: Hamlet's dying lines, comparing death to a stern officer of the law.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 5 the dying Hamlet says 'this fell sergeant, death, / Is strict in his arrest': death is pictured as a cruel officer, 'fell' meaning cruel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's day the officer who arrested debtors and offenders held this rank, so death is pictured as one making an arrest.

clue.text: Tempting if burdensome job for the judge

definitions.meaning: to tempt once meant to test, and a burdensome task is a testing one
a judge hears a case in court

explanation.surface: A tempting but heavy task assigned to a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tempting' uses the old sense of tempt, to put to the test, as in the Bible's 'God did tempt Abraham'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something testing or tiresome is wearing, and hearing a case in court is what a judge does to a defendant.

clue.text: The Observer vis-a vis The Listener ?

definitions.text: The Observer vis-a vis The Listener ?

parts.words: The Observer vis-a vis The Listener
parts.note: an instrument that observes and is pointed at the ear, the organ that listens

explanation.surface: Two British periodicals, The Observer newspaper and The Listener magazine, set face to face.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday newspaper and The Listener was the BBC's weekly magazine, but here the observer is a doctor's instrument held face to face with the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's instrument for looking into the ear canal observes the organ of hearing.
